description: We are a team from Anglo-Chinese School (Independent)
summary:
Neo Universe – Earth Information Jukebox
We developed an interactive, accessible Earth Information Jukebox comprising three interconnected Github repositories. Sonificator is a Rust-based audio engine that analyses video frames, translating visual properties such as brightness, colour, spatial position and movement into dynamically generated stereo music. Sonificator Studio provides a browser-based demonstration, integrating the engine through WebAssembly to sonify videos in real time while displaying live visual analysis. Finally, our Earth Information Jukebox Website presents NASA's Earth visualisations through an interactive 3D globe, allowing users to explore datasets alongside their generated sound.
Together, these components address the challenge of making Earth science accessible beyond visualisation alone. By translating visual information into sound and incorporating screen-reader support, keyboard navigation and accessibility controls, we create a more inclusive, engaging and multi-sensory learning experience. This matters because understanding our changing planet should not depend solely on the ability to see but should be an experience that more people can access, explore and connect with.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?

Neo Universe is a web experience where NASA’s Earth visualizations become music, so blind and low-vision people can explore the same data as sighted viewers. The home page is a spinning 3D Earth: NASA Earth Information Center datasets (night lights, sea-surface temperature, aerosols, air quality, ocean flow, lightning, atmospheric rivers, forest height) glow as lights on the planet, and the site’s sections — how it sounds, about, quiz, dataset list — orbit it as moons, so whatever spins past you is what you choose. Selecting a topic opens a video panel and starts the sonificator: a Rust audio engine compiled to WebAssembly that reads the video’s frames in real time and composes a soundtrack from the pixels. Color salience drives the energy and groove, horizontal feature movement maps to stereo pan and melodic motifs, vertical movement changes register and timbre, and the spread of colored motion controls how dense the arpeggios become. Texture analysis of the color palette also nudges the key and chord progression, all locked to a C major pentatonic scale so the output is always musical. Live meters under the video show what the engine currently “hears,” and there is a pill-shaped activity meter similar to those on accessibility dashboards.

What benefits does it have?

The core one is equal access: the same NASA visualizations that delight sighted users become audible and explorable without any extra equipment — a browser and speakers or headphones are enough. It runs entirely client-side (the audio is synthesized in slots of a Web Audio context fed by WASM), so there is no server, no account, and no cost. The build pipeline fetches NASA’s original videos and transcodes them locally, so the site works even where NASA’s servers are unreachable or lack CORS headers. It’s also useful as a teaching aid: hearing ocean currents speed up or the sun’s glow intensify makes a dataset’s behavior memorable in a way a chart is not.

What is the intended impact of the project?

About 2.2 billion people worldwide live with some degree of vision impairment, and data visualization — NASA’s specialty — is almost entirely theirs to miss. We want demonstrating that a science visualization can be fully experienced through sound, with zero interaction cost for blind users, and that this pattern can be reused for any video of data, not just ours. Longer-term, the sonificator engine is a standalone, reusable component that could sit in front of any agency’s or lab’s imagery.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

The sonificator engine is written in Rust, compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen, and plays through the Web Audio API, with Vorbis synthesis keeping quantization timing right inside the browser. The site itself is vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS with three.js (WebGL) for the 3D globe — no front-end framework, so it stays light. Tooling: FFmpeg and curl in shell scripts for the video pipeline, Nix flakes for a reproducible dev environment, and GitHub Actions deploying static files to GitHub Pages. Testing was done with the NVDA screen reader and keyboard only. Hardware: ordinary laptops; nothing beyond a standard GitHub-hosted CI runner.

How is your project creative?

Two ways. First, the interface metaphor: the site is a literal universe — datasets as lights on the planet, sections as moons orbiting it — so navigation is also a geography you can explore rather than a menu you scan. Second, the sonification itself: instead of mapping data values to fixed pitches (the common approach), the engine composes groove-based music from the look of the frames — color salience for energy, motion for pan, register, and density — so a visualization’s composition becomes a composition in music. A busy, colorful scene sounds energetic and dense; a quiet one breathes. Even monochrome data gets a musical fallback based on motion.

What factors did your team consider?

Accessibility first and foremost: keyboard-complete navigation, ARIA labels, definitions tested with NVDA, and no reliance on color anywhere. Performance: everything is procedural (synthesized), and the server hosts small local H.264 copies of the source videos so audio decoding never depends on NASA’s servers or CORS. Fairness in the sonification: a hue-agnostic salience measure was used so sonifications do not depend on a dataset using specific colors. Robustness: the build is idempotent, cached, and re-runnable, and the fallback default video ships in the repository so the site always has at least one working experience. And honesty of the data: the meters and “how it sounds” documentation describe what the engine measures, so users are never guessing what a sound corresponds to.
